_Article_

## Enhancing Pre-Service Teachers’ AI-TPACK Through Sustainable Development Goals: A Mixed-Methods Study on AI-Supported Web 2.0 Tools

**Bayram** **Gökbulut**

Department of Educational Sciences, Eregli˘ Faculty of Education, Zonguldak Bulent Ecevit University, Eregli 67350, Zonguldak, Turkey; bayram.gokbulut@beun.edu.tr

**Abstract**

Rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, coupled with UNESCO’s Education 2030 vision, necessitate a re-evaluation of teachers’ technological and pedagog- ical competencies aligned with sustainability goals. This study investigates the impact of pre-service teachers developing digital materials within the framework of the Sustain- able Development Goals (SDGs) using AI and AI-supported Web 2.0 tools (e.g., ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Alayna, Padlet, Canva, Kahoot) on their Artificial Intelligence Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK) levels. Employing an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, the research was conducted with 31 pre-service teachers over a 10-week applied training period. Data were collected via the AI-TPACK Scale and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative findings revealed that the applied training signifi- cantly enhanced the pre-service teachers’ Pedagogical Knowledge (PK), AI-Technological Knowledge (AI-TK), Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), and overall AI-TPACK levels. However, no statistically significant difference was observed in the Content Knowledge (CK) dimension. Qualitative data demonstrated that AI-supported tools made the learning environment more engaging and efficient, concretized abstract sustainability concepts, and bolstered the pre-service teachers’ digital self-confidence. Consequently, this study establishes that integrating AI tools into SDG education is an effective strategy for cultivat- ing pre-service teachers’ technopedagogical competencies, empowering them to perceive technology as a facilitator of professional development rather than an instructional barrier.

**Keywords:** artificial intelligence; sustainable development goals; AI-TPACK; teacher education; Web 2.0 tools

Widely used Web 2.0 tools such as Canva, Kahoot, and Padlet offer teachers unique opportunities for content creation and differentiated instruction with the AI support they have gained \[[6\]](#references). These tools play a critical role in developing students’ writing skills and concretizing abstract concepts \[[7,8\]](#references). These technologies, which improve teachers’ material preparation skills, make educational processes more efficient \[[9\]](#references) and transform the teacher’s role from a mere transmitter of knowledge to a learning designer and digital guide \[[10\]](#references). Therefore, in this transformation process, teachers’ ability to use AI systems effectively, both technologically and pedagogically, is of vital importance \[[11\]](#references).

The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) carries out comprehensive studies on the use of AI in education, the development of teacher competencies, and increasing the quality of education. In line with its 2030 goals, UNESCO positions education as a fundamental human right and a driving force for sustainable development. In particular, Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) has identified “ensuring inclusive and equitable quality education and promoting lifelong learning opportunities for all” as a global priority \[[12\]](#references). The AI Competency Framework for Teachers published by UNESCO \[[13\]](#references) redefines teachers’ AI literacy not only with technical skills but also within the axis of ethics, human rights, and sustainability \[[12,13\]](#references). AI has strategic importance with its potential to reduce inequalities in education, personalize learning, and optimize management systems \[[14\]](#references). However, the complex and multi- dimensional nature of the concept of sustainability causes teachers to experience difficulties in conveying this subject. To overcome this challenge and achieve sustainability goals, the effective use of technology \[[15\]](#references) and the presence of expert teachers who master these technologies are required. On the other hand, the unconscious use of AI-supported tools carries the risk of reinforcing existing biases and damaging equality of opportunity in education \[16\].

# 2. Literature Review

## _2.1._ _Artificial_ _Intelligence_ _and_ _Web_ _2.0_ _Tools_ The technological transformation brought by the 21st century has moved educational

environments away from traditional teaching methods, allowing them to evolve into a digital ecosystem where the student is an active participant and content creator. Web

2.0 technologies, located at the center of this transformation, lead a paradigm shift in education by increasing information sharing, collaboration, and interaction among users. Web 2.0 tools positively affect students’ class participation, motivation, and academic achievements \[17\]. The use of these technologies in educational settings plays a critical role in putting theoretical knowledge into practice and gaining digital literacy skills \[[11\]](#references). In particular, applications such as Canva, Prezi, Kahoot, and Mentimeter stand out as effective Web 2.0 tools that support student-centered approaches, keep interest alive, and allow for the personalization of learning materials \[18\]. These tools make significant contributions to students’ collaborative working competencies, problem-solving skills, and the concretization of abstract concepts \[[7,1](#references)9\]. In Web 2.0 applications, individuals can produce, update, and publish their own content without having any technical knowledge, enabling them to transition from being web readers to web literates \[20,21\].

Educational technologies have moved beyond Web 2.0 and gained a new dimension with AI integration. AI has become a transformative force in education with its potential to improve instructional design, personalize student experiences, and facilitate administrative processes. Parallel to the developments in AI technologies, the vast majority of companies developing Web 2.0 tools have ensured the integration of AI tools into their systems. Thus, the concept of Web 2.0 has transformed into the concept of AI-supported AI-Web 2.0. With

AI support, many important tasks such as content preparation, assessment, and material creation in educational environments have become easier \[[6\]](#references). While AI-supported tools offer personalized learning paths to students, they relieve the administrative burden on teachers, allowing them to focus more on pedagogical processes \[22\]. For teachers to use AI- supported Web 2.0 tools effectively in education, possessing only technological knowledge is not sufficient; they must also possess “Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge” (TPACK), which blends this technology with pedagogical and content knowledge \[23\].

Recent studies indicate that the readiness of teachers and pre-service teachers for AI- supported tools directly affects their pedagogical integration skills. For instance, Uzumcu and Acilmis \[24\] found that as pre-service teachers’ individual innovativeness levels in- creased, they used AI-supported Web 2.0 tools (such as Google Arts and Culture) in their lesson plans in a more interactive manner suitable for pedagogical goals. However, the literature also emphasizes that teachers have significant deficiencies in this regard. Ya¸sar and Vuran \[[6\]](#references) stated that teachers do not have sufficient knowledge about AI-supported tools and need face-to-face workshops to integrate these tools into instructional processes. From the perspective of AI-TPACK development, the importance of discipline-specific applications is increasing. While Kul and Canoglu˘ \[25\] emphasized that tools such as Note- bookLM and AI-supported Kahoot contribute to the reinforcement of knowledge in German teaching, Najibufahmi et al. \[[9\]](#references) reported that the use of AI-supported Canva in mathe- matics teaching improves teachers’ teaching skills. Similarly, Çöçen and Yapıcıoglu˘ \[26\] drew attention to the fact that AI-supported Web 2.0 activities improve critical thinking in the discussion of socio-scientific issues. Awang et al. \[27\] stated that Web 2.0 and AI integration have the potential to offer personalized learning experiences to students and create intelligent tutoring systems, suggesting that future research should focus on the ethical dimensions of this integration.

In the context of this study, it is essential to draw a conceptual distinction between traditional Web 2.0 tools and the ‘AI-supported Web 2.0 tools’ employed in the intervention. While traditional Web 2.0 technologies rely on ‘user-generated content’ where the user manually inputs text and designs layouts from scratch, the core feature of the tools used in this study (e.g., Canva Magic Design-Education, Padlet AI-Basic, Prezi-Basic, Kahoot-Basic, Alayna 3.0) is AI-enabled generative creation.

This distinction represents a fundamental shift in the theoretical framework of instruc- tional design:

1. From Manual Construction to Generative Co-Creation: In traditional tools, the teacher is the sole constructor of the material. In AI-supported tools, the teacher acts as a ‘prompt engineer’ who guides generative algorithms to produce lesson plans, visuals, or assessments.
2. Role Transformation: The teacher’s role shifts from a ‘manual designer’ spending hours on formatting to a ‘curator’ and ‘pedagogical editor’ who evaluates and refines AI-generated outputs.

Therefore, when the term ‘AI-supported Web 2.0 tools’ is used in this study, it refers to Web 2.0 platforms integrated with a generative artificial intelligence infrastructure that automates the digital material production process, rather than digital materials prepared by the teacher using traditional Web 2.0 tools.

## _2.2._ _Artificial_ _Intelligence_ _and_ _Sustainability_ _in_ _Education_ UNESCO evaluates the use of AI technology in education not only as a technological

innovation but also as a tool for ethical, inclusive, and sustainable transformation. The organization’s “Education 2030” vision recommends the strategic and responsible use of AI technologies in ensuring inclusive and quality education for all, in line with Sustainable

Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) \[28\]. In this context, UNESCO emphasizes that AI-supported educational applications must be human-centered, ethically based, and fully compatible with sustainable development goals \[[12\]](#references). Specifically within the scope of SDG 4, the role of AI in education is defined within the axis of personalizing learning processes to adapt to different learning styles, creating accessible educational environments for disadvantaged groups, supporting teachers’ professional development, and making measurement and assessment processes fairer and data-based. In achieving these goals, teachers possessing AI literacy and addressing technology together with its pedagogical and ethical dimensions are stated as critical requirements \[[13\]](#references). Based on this necessity, the AI Competency Framework for Teachers published by UNESCO in 2024 serves as a comprehensive guide developed to enable teachers to use AI technologies consciously, ethically, and pedagogically effectively. This model does not limit teacher competencies to technical skills only; it addresses the process with a holistic approach involving pedagogical, ethical, and social responsibility dimensions \[[13\]](#references). Four key competency areas are identified in the said framework: AI Literacy, Pedagogical Integration, Ethics, Safety and Human Rights, and Professional Development and Lifelong Learning.

## _2.3._ _AI-TPACK_ _Framework_ The theoretical basis of the TPACK framework relies on the concept of “Pedagogical

Content Knowledge” (PCK), which is a synthesis of Pedagogical Knowledge (PK) and Con- tent Knowledge (CK), proposed by Shulman \[29\]. According to Shulman, PCK represents the most effective methods, strategies, and forms of representation necessary to convey specific content to students. Mishra and Koehler \[30\] expanded this framework put forward by Shulman by adding the “Technological Knowledge” (TK) dimension, introducing the “Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge” (TPACK) model to the literatüre. The TPACK model, built on the intersection of three basic components, technological knowledge (TK), pedagogical knowledge (PK), and content knowledge (CK), has formed the basis for many academic studies in the field of educational technologies. However, the fact that AI technologies influence every field, including education, today has created a need to update the existing framework. In this context, Celik \[31\] reevaluated the TPACK model together with AI dynamics and proposed the “AI-TPACK” model (Figure [1)](#23-ai-tpack-framework-the-theoretical-basis-of-the-tpack-framework-relies-on-the-concept-of-pedagogical). Celik \[31\] explains the rationale for this new model with the thesis that as teachers’ AI literacy levels increase, they can reflect their pedagogical knowledge in teaching processes much more effectively.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

 **Figure** **1.** TPACK and AI-TPACK framework Celik \[31\].

According to the model specified in Figure [1,](#23-ai-tpack-framework-the-theoretical-basis-of-the-tpack-framework-relies-on-the-concept-of-pedagogical) the AI-supported TPACK model consists of AI-TK, AI-TPK, AI-TCK, and AI-TPACK components. The increase in the use of AI tools, which offer new pedagogical opportunities in teaching and learning processes today,

has caused radical changes in teachers’ teaching and students’ learning styles \[27–29\]. Depending on this rapid development of AI tools, teachers may encounter certain difficul- ties during the integration process into education \[32\]. Teachers’ ability to adapt to this process primarily depends on their being competent AI literates. Teachers who do not have sufficient AI literacy struggle to integrate these tools effectively into their lessons and cannot fully benefit from the educational potential of AI \[[1\]](#references). When viewed on a global scale, courses on AI usage for teachers have started to appear in the curricula in the education systems of China, South Korea, Austria, and the European Union. Despite this, there is still no clarity regarding the full integration of AI into the education system, and how to teach this technology, especially at the K-12 level, continues to be debated \[33,34\]. Consequently, although AI tools are developing rapidly at the K-12 level, teachers’ knowledge and skills regarding integrating these tools into pedagogical processes remain at a limited level \[31\].

## _2.4._ _Problem_ _Statement_ Sustainability is not only a global educational concern but also a strategic element

contributing to AI-focused curriculum transformation \[35\]. However, sustainability topics have not been sufficiently addressed in the process of integration into educational curricula due to their inherently complex nature. This situation increases the need for diversified pedagogical approaches in teaching the concepts in question \[36\]. Although teachers play a key role in meeting these needs, certain difficulties are experienced in current teacher competencies and integration processes \[37\]. To overcome these difficulties, there is a need for TPACK-based applied training for pre-service teachers \[34\].

Sustainability education is a field that requires technology-supported, special ped- agogy and teaching methods \[[15,3](#references)5,38\]. At this point, AI-supported Web 2.0 tools can offer an effective solution for teachers and pre-service teachers \[39\]. It is possible to utilize the AI-TPACK model for these tools to be used efficiently in educational environments. The successful implementation of the AI-TPACK model depends on the quality of the education to be given to pre-service teachers during their undergraduate studies. Today, young pre-service teachers receiving undergraduate education have higher familiarity with AI technologies compared to in-service teachers \[40\]. Integrating AI applications into un- dergraduate education to cover the TPACK framework will make significant contributions to both the adoption of AI-TPACK \[41\] and the concretization of abstract and complex concepts in sustainability subjects.

In recent years, a significant increase has been observed in the literature regarding stud- ies examining teachers’ readiness and competencies for artificial intelligence integration within the AI-TPACK framework. For instance, Ning et al. \[42\] examined the relationship between AI-TPACK components and revealed the complexity of developing non-technical knowledge types. Similarly, Reyes-Rojas et al. \[41\] conceptualized the ‘Intelligent-TPACK’ approach for pre-service teachers’ integration processes, while Tram \[43\] explored the relationship between technology acceptance models and AI-TPACK. Furthermore, Hava and Babayigit˘ \[44\] empirically demonstrated the predictive effect of digital proficiency on AI-TPACK. However, most of these recent studies have been limited to descriptive or corre- lational survey models. As stated by Koçulu \[45\], there is a need for applied intervention studies to enable teachers to overcome the pedagogical challenges they experience while planning Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) topics.

Consequently, this study aims to fill this gap in the literature and go beyond merely testing the effectiveness of a training program. The research seeks to demonstrate how the AI-TPACK framework can be concretely operationalized into an actionable teacher professional development model aimed at SDG teaching. While existing literature is mostly descriptive, this study presents a unique value proposition by showing how AI-supported

‘digital material creation’ serves as a bridge between abstract sustainability goals and concrete classroom practices. By integrating AI tools into the design process, the study proposes a practical pathway for transforming pre-service teachers from passive consumers of technology into active designers of sustainable education.

# 3. Method

## _3.1._ _Research_ _Design_ The research was conducted using a mixed-methods research approach. Mixed meth-

ods research is a method in which qualitative and quantitative data are used together \[46\]. An explanatory sequential design was adopted in the study, where quantitative data is collected first, and then quantitative data is supported by qualitative data \[47\].

In the quantitative dimension of the research, a single-group pretest-posttest experi- mental design was used \[48\]. With this method, the aim was to reveal the development in pre-service teachers’ AI-supported technopedagogical content knowledge levels. The qualitative dimension of the research was conducted as a case study, which allows for a multifaceted examination of an event \[49\]. The “Artificial Intelligence Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK) Scale” was used as the pretest-posttest in the research. After the post-test was administered, pre-service teachers’ opinions regarding the implementations carried out were obtained using a semi-structured interview form.

## _3.2._ _Study_ _Group_ This research was carried out with 2nd-year students studying at the Faculty of

Education of a state university in Turkey during the 2024–2025 academic year. The study group of the research consists of a total of 31 pre-service teachers, 22 female and 9 male. The implementation process was conducted within the scope of the “Instructional Technologies” course, where pre-service teachers gain theoretical and practical competencies regarding the use of technology in educational environments. Purposive sampling, one of the non- probability sampling methods, was preferred in determining the participants. Accordingly, pre-service teachers who were actively taking the Instructional Technologies course during the period the research was conducted were included in the scope of the study.

## _3.3._ _Data_ _Collection_ The “Artificial Intelligence Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge Scale” (AI-

TPACK) was used to collect quantitative data in the research. Originally developed by Ning et al. \[42\], this scale was adapted into Turkish by Canbazoglu˘ et al. \[50\]. The scale consists of a total of 37 items and 7 sub-factors. These factors are: Content Knowledge (CK—5 items), Pedagogical Knowledge (PK—6 items), AI-Technological Knowledge (AI-TK—5 items), Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK—6 items), AI-Technological Content Knowledge (AI-TCK—6 items), AI-Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (AI-TPK—6 items), and AI-Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK—5 items). The Cronbach Alpha internal consistency coefficients calculated in the Turkish adaptation study of the scale were reported as follows: CK: 0.873, PK: 0.888, AI-TK: 0.954, PCK: 0.928, AI-TCK: 0.973, AI-TPK: 0.970, and AI-TPACK: 0.946. The reliability coefficients calculated in this research are as follows: CK: 0.717, PK: 0.860, AI-TK: 0.640, PCK: 0.843, AI-TCK: 0.900, AI-TPK: 0.904, and AI-TPACK: 0.823.

In the qualitative dimension of the research, a semi-structured interview form was used to determine the pre-service teachers’ opinions regarding the completed implementations. While preparing the interview questions, the items and basic factors of the AI-TPACK scale were taken as a reference. To ensure the content and language validity of the prepared draft questions, the opinions of two academicians who are experts in the field of educational

sciences were sought, and the form was finalized. The questions directed to the pre-service teachers are as follows:

1. Do you think AI-supported Web 2.0 tools contribute to learning environments? Why?
2. Do you think these tools contribute to your content knowledge? Why?
3. Do you think these tools contribute to your pedagogical knowledge? Why?
4. Do you think these tools contribute to your technological knowledge? Why? The pre-service teachers’ answers to the qualitative questions were collected using the

Web 2.0 tool named Padlet. The responses given by the pre-service teachers to the questions are seen in Figure [2.](#34-implementation-the-implementation-process-of-the-research-was-carried-out-within-the-scope-of-the)

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

## _3.4._ _Implementation_ The implementation process of the research was carried out within the scope of the

compulsory “Instructional Technologies” course in the 2nd-year curriculum of the Faculty of Education. In this study, which lasted a total of 10 weeks, pre-service teachers were provided with theoretical and practical training on the use of AI and AI-supported Web 2.0 tools. During the implementation process, pre-service teachers were expected to develop digital materials suitable for the UNESCO 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). While determining the material topics, the Social Studies and Science curricula taught at the secondary school level in Turkey were taken as a basis, and the learning outcomes of these courses were associated with the SDG targets.

The main purpose of this process was to develop pre-service teachers’ technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge (TPACK) and to increase their skills in integrating artificial intelligence tools into educational environments. The process carried out for this purpose is shown in Figure 3.

As seen in Figure 3, in the first stage, the AI-TPACK scale was administered as a pre-test. Subsequently, during the ten-week training and material development phase, in addition to generative AI tools such as ChatGPT-4.0, DeepSeek V3.2, and Alayna 3.0, Web 2.0 tools with AI infrastructure such as Padlet-Basic, Kahoot-Basic, Prezi-Basic, Canva- Education, and Mentimeter-free were effectively used. Pre-service teachers worked in five separate groups. The digital materials developed using these tools were subjected to peer assessment every week. Pre-service teachers presented the digital materials they developed in the classroom environment weekly, and these were evaluated by their peers in the dimensions of ‘content, pedagogy, and technology’. In this process, the candidates had

the opportunity to revise their materials in line with the feedback they received from their peers. Thus, the quality of the developed materials was increased, and faulty constructions in the learning process were corrected instantly. The study was completed in a total period of 10 weeks, with two lesson hours (45 min + 45 min) per week. The weekly training plan is presented in Table 1.

Pre-service teachers designed digital materials suitable for the secondary school cur- riculum by benefiting from various Web 2.0 and AI tools. In the material development process, educational contents were structured based on the topic titles within the scope of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Thanks to this implementation process, candi- dates found the opportunity to develop their AI-TPACK competencies through practice by integrating their technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge within the axis of artificial intelligence.

## _3.5._ _Ethical_ _Procedures_ Before starting the implementation process, pre-service teachers were informed about

the purpose of the study. It was explained that participation in the study was based on voluntariness. Pre-service teachers were informed that they could withdraw from the study unconditionally at any point in the study. The real identities of the pre-service teachers were not included in any part of the study. It was confirmed that the research did not pose an ethical problem with the ethics committee report of Zonguldak Bülent Ecevit University Human Research Ethics Committee dated 21 February 2025 and protocol number 100/567664.

## _3.6._ _Data_ _Analysis_ Analysis of Quantitative Data: Before starting the data analysis process, it was exam-

ined whether the data set met the normality assumptions. As a result of the tests performed, it was determined that the data showed a normal distribution. Accordingly, the Paired Samples _t_-test, one of the parametric tests, was used to compare the pre-test and post-test scores obtained from the AI-TPACK scale.

# Analysis of Qualitative Data: The content analysis technique was adopted in analyzing the qualitative data obtained in the research. The MAXQDA 24.10 qualitative data analysis program was utilized in the process of coding and categorizing the data. To ensure coding reliability, the data were analyzed independently by two different field experts; then, the created codes and themes were compared, and similar structures were gathered under appropriate categories. The inter-coder reliability coefficient was calculated using the formula \[Reliability = Agreement/(Agreement + Disagreement)\] suggested by \[51\]. The analysis followed an inductive approach grounded in the constant comparative method. Beyond merely calculating frequencies, the researchers engaged in an iterative coding process to identify patterns and relationships between themes. Initial codes were grouped into categories, and axial coding was applied to understand how different experiential factors (e.g., environmental engagement, technological confidence) interacted to drive the development of AI-TPACK competencies. As a result of the calculation made, it was determined that the agreement coefficient was over 90%, and this rate is considered sufficient for the reliability of the research. When presenting the analysis results, direct quotations were included to support the findings and reflect the participants’ opinions exactly as they were.

4. **Results**

In this study, pre-service teachers were enabled to design digital materials using AI-supported Web 2.0 tools to develop their AI-TPACK competencies. The contents of these developed materials were selected from the topic titles within the scope of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) included in the 6th and 7th-grade Social Studies and Science curricula in Turkey. During the data collection process, the “AI-TPACK Scale” was administered to the pre-service teachers as a pre-test and post-test before and after the implementation. Throughout the process, the digital materials developed by the candidates were subjected to both peer assessment and researcher assessment, and necessary feedback was provided. At the end of the implementation, pre-service teachers’ opinions were consulted to examine the development in their AI-TPACK levels in greater depth. The obtained quantitative and qualitative data were evaluated and analyzed using a holistic approach.

## _4.1._ _Findings_ _Regarding_ _Pre-Service_ _Teachers’_ _AI-Supported_ _Technological_ _Pedagogical_ _Content_ _Knowledge_ _Levels_

The Paired Samples _t_-test was used to determine whether there was a significant difference between the pre-service teachers’ AI-TPACK pre-test and post-test average scores. The test results are given in Table [2.](#41-findings-regarding-pre-service-teachers-ai-supported-technological-pedagogical-content-knowledge-levels)

When Table [2](#41-findings-regarding-pre-service-teachers-ai-supported-technological-pedagogical-content-knowledge-levels) is examined, it is observed that there is no statistically significant difference between the pre-service teachers’ pre-test (_X_ = 3.49) and post-test (_X_ = 3.65) mean scores in the Content Knowledge (CK) dimension (_p_ \> 0.05). The effect size for this dimension was found to be small (_d_ = 0.33).

In contrast, a significant increase was detected in favor of the post-test in all other sub-dimensions of the scale (_p_ \< 0.05). To determine the magnitude of these significant differences, Cohen’s _d_ effect sizes were calculated. The findings are as follows:

In the Pedagogical Knowledge (PK) dimension, the average rose from (_X_ = 3.73) to (_X_ = 4.02), showing a significant difference with a medium effect size (_d_ = 0.41). In the AI-Technological Knowledge (AI-TK) dimension, the average increased from (_X_ = 3.39) to (_X_ = 3.88), indicating a medium-to-large effect (_d_ = 0.69). The most substantial improve- ments were observed in the integrated TPACK components. In the Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) dimension, the score rose from (_X_ = 3.40) to (_X_ = 3.97) with a large effect size (_d_ = 0.76). Similarly, the AI-Technological Content Knowledge (AI-TCK) dimension saw an increase from (_X_ = 3.17) to (_X_ = 3.87), representing a large effect (_d_ = 0.90). The highest gains were recorded in the AI-Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (AI-TPK) dimension, rising from (_X_ = 3.12) to (_X_ = 3.94) with a very large effect (_d_ = 0.97), and in the overall AI-TPACK dimension, which increased from (_X_ = 3.12) to (_X_ = 3.93) (_d_ = 0.93).

In light of these findings, it can be stated that the implemented training provided not only statistically significant but also practically substantial improvements in the pre- service teachers’ technopedagogical competencies, particularly in the intersectional do- mains (AI-TCK, AI-TPK, and AI-TPACK), while the impact on Content Knowledge (CK) remained limited.

## _4.2._ _Opinions_ _of_ _Pre-Service_ _Teachers_ _Regarding_ _AI-Supported_ _Digital_ _Material_ _Preparation_ _Processes_

Qualitative opinions were sought to examine the AI-TPACK gains and experiences acquired by the pre-service teachers at the end of the 10-week implementation process in depth. In this context, four open-ended questions were directed to the participants; the obtained data were analyzed using the content analysis method, and codes and themes were created (Figure [10)](#42-opinions-of-pre-service-teachers-regarding-ai-supported-digital-material-preparation-processes).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

 **Figure** **10.** Main themes formed under AI-TPACK.

As a result of the analysis, four main themes were determined under the AI-TPACK framework: Learning Environment, Technological Knowledge, Pedagogical Knowledge, and Content Knowledge.

Under the “Learning Environment” main theme, a total of ten codes were gener- ated (Figure [11)](#42-opinions-of-pre-service-teachers-regarding-ai-supported-digital-material-preparation-processes). These codes, according to their frequencies, are: fun learning (_f_ = 13), visual/creative content (_f_ = 12), effective learning (_f_ = 10), active participation (_f_ = 9), per- manent learning (_f_ = 7), personalized instruction (_f_ = 6), collaboration (_f_ = 4), gamification (_f_ = 4), motivation (_f_ = 2), and interaction (_f_ = 4).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

 **Figure** **11.** Codes formed under the Learning Environment main theme.

When Figure [11](#42-opinions-of-pre-service-teachers-regarding-ai-supported-digital-material-preparation-processes) is examined, pre-service teachers emphasized that AI-supported Web 2.0 tools made learning environments more enjoyable. Some of the participants’ opinions are as follows: “Tools like Padlet, Canva, Kahoot, and Mentimeter attract students’ attention while making learning more fun and permanent.” (S7); “I can prepare magnificent presentations just by entering the topic title into Prezi.” (S2). Participants also stated that they could create creative and attention-grabbing visual materials with these tools: “When I write a prompt with ChatGPT, I become aware of situations that did not come to my mind or that I did not pay attention to. This causes me to think more deeply about that subject and directs me to creativity.” (S6); “I can plan lessons in a way that is suitable for the student level, creative, and effective.” (S12).

Opinions regarding the fact that the tools support effective learning are as follows: “Thanks to Canva, I prepare my presentations in a more effective, remarkable, and vivid way. Not just presentations; I can produce materials on many subjects such as lesson plans and posters.” (S11); “I can prepare remarkable visuals with Canva and effective questions according to the nature of the subject with ChatGPT.” (S4).

Candidates stated that these tools ensure students’ active participation in the lesson and support collaborative learning: “These tools do not just transmit information, they also make the learning process active. Every teacher should use these tools that directly affect participation in the lesson.” (S9); “Padlet facilitates idea sharing and collaboration; it makes group work efficient. Thus, students actively collaborate with their friends instead of just listening.” (S12, S19).

Opinions regarding permanent learning and personalized instruction are as follows: “Activities such as Q&A, polls, and word clouds created with Mentimeter reinforce the learned subject and ensure permanent learning.” (S10); “ChatGPT answers the questions we ask instantly. I can prepare separate questions for each student and evaluate them individually.” (S20).

Under the “Pedagogical Knowledge” main theme, five codes were determined (Figure 12). These codes are listed as: Planning (_f_ = 7), Student-Centered Teaching (_f_ = 7), Feedback (_f_ = 5), Assessment (_f_ = 4), and Differentiated Instruction (_f_ = 4).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

 **Figure** **12.** Codes located under the Pedagogical Knowledge main theme.

Pre-service teachers stated that AI-supported tools contribute to lesson planning and student-centered teaching processes: “It is quite easy to prepare a visual lesson plan using Padlet’s AI support. I can easily make differentiated lesson plans with this tool.” (S9, S4); “While these tools increase students’ active participation in the lesson, they make the learning process more effective by offering materials suitable for different learning styles. We can plan the educational process as student-centered.” (S7, S19).

Attention was drawn to the functionality of the Mentimeter tool, especially in feedback and evaluation processes: “Mentimeter is very functional in terms of receiving instant feedback from students and seeing how much they have grasped the subject. With this tool, we can ask students questions and get instant answers.” (S16, S17). It was also stated that these tools gave pre-service teachers different perspectives: “AI tools enabled me to develop different perspectives. By leading to new ideas and thoughts, they helped me find very different solutions to problems.” (S6, S8, S14).

Under the “Content Knowledge” main theme, the codes Fast Access to Information (_f_ = 13), Time Saving (_f_ = 9), Different Perspective (_f_ = 7), Deepening Knowledge (_f_ = 6), and Simplifying Topics (_f_ = 5) were formed (Figure 13).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

 **Figure** **13.** Codes located under the Content Knowledge main theme.

Pre-service teachers stated that access to information accelerated and the content was enriched thanks to artificial intelligence tools: “With AI-supported Web 2.0 tools, informa- tion can be accessed quickly, and complex subjects can be made more understandable and simple. This both saves time and allows for in-depth learning.” (S4, S6, S8, S10).

Under the “Technological Knowledge” main theme, four basic codes emerged (Figure [14)](#43-synthesis-of-qualitative-findings-while-the-themes-presented-above-describe-independent-dimensions-of-the-partici-). These are: Efficiency and Ease (_f_ = 9), Exploring New Tools (_f_ = 8), Self-Confidence (_f_ = 8), and Digital Literacy (_f_ = 4).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Figure** **14.** Codes located under the Technological Knowledge main theme.

Participants expressed that their self-confidence regarding technology use increased and their digital competencies developed: “I used to have difficulty preparing presentations. Now I can design activities more easily and quickly. I have learned how to use technology more efficiently.”; “I had not used technology this effectively before. Although it seemed difficult at first, as I applied what I learned, I realized that it was not that difficult, and my self-confidence increased.” (S5); “By using these tools, my ability to solve technology- related problems developed, I gained the habit of following innovative technologies, and my digital literacy level increased.” (S3, S7).

## _4.3._ _Synthesis_ _of_ _Qualitative_ _Findings_ While the themes presented above describe independent dimensions of the partici-

pants’ experiences, the relationship between these themes reveals a specific mechanism of change for AI-TPACK development. As illustrated by the findings, the process follows a cyclical interaction rather than a linear path.

1. Trigger (Engaging Environment): The visual richness and interactive nature of AI tools transformed the perception of the learning environment from ‘static’ to ‘fun’ and ‘engaging’. This positive emotional atmosphere lowered pre-service teachers’ resistance to new technology.
2. Catalyst (Technological Confidence): The ease of use and ‘efficiency’ provided by generative AI acted as a catalyst. Participants realized they could produce high- quality materials without advanced technical skills, which significantly boosted their ‘Technological Self-Confidence’.
3. Process (Pedagogical Reflection): This confidence enabled them to move beyond technical concerns and focus on pedagogical goals. The ability to ‘save time’ allowed candidates to engage in deeper ‘Pedagogical Reflection’, focusing on student-centered planning and differentiated instruction.

Beyond this cyclical mechanism, the findings suggest a fundamental shift in the communicational role of the teacher. The transition from manual material production to AI-assisted design places the pre-service teacher in a new form of ‘pedagogical mediation’. In this process, the teacher does not merely transmit information but acts as a critical filter between the generative capabilities of AI and the cognitive needs of the student.

The qualitative emphasis on ‘visual/creative content’ and ‘simplifying topics’ indicates that candidates are using AI as a translator—converting complex SDG concepts into ac- cessible educational codes. This implies that AI-TPACK development involves not just technical proficiency but a communicative competence in prompting AI to serve specific pedagogical narratives.

5. **Discussion**

This study examined the effect of pre-service teachers developing digital materials using AI (ChatGPT, DeepSeek) and AI-supported Web 2.0 tools (Padlet, Canva, Kahoot, Mentimeter, Prezi, Alayna) within the context of UNESCO 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) on their AI-TPACK levels. The findings obtained are discussed below in comparison with the relevant literature, in light of the statistical results from quantitative data and themes from qualitative interviews. Rather than treating SDGs as a thematic background, this study operationalized sustainability education through observable peda- gogical outputs. Each SDG was translated into concrete learning outcomes and assessed indirectly via AI-TPACK dimensions, such as lesson planning quality, assessment design, and material differentiation. Thus, sustainability was embedded not only as content but as a measurable component of pre-service teachers’ instructional competence.

Qualitative findings indicated that AI-supported Web 2.0 tools (Padlet, Kahoot, Canva, Mentimeter, etc.) rendered the learning environment “fun”, “visually rich”, and “inter- active”. Pre-service teachers’ emphasis on gamification and collaboration suggests that these tools increase student motivation and active participation through AI integration. In qualitative interviews, candidates stated that their technological self-confidence increased, coded as “efficiency”, “ease”, and “discovering new tools”. Pre-service teachers stated that these tools increased students’ active participation in the lesson and provided motivation. Studies in the literature support this finding. AI takes on roles beyond motivation and speaking opportunities in education \[52\]. Gocen and Aydemir \[53\] note that AI offers new opportunities to students that traditional classroom environments cannot offer. Pre-service teachers prepare engaging and fun content with Web 2.0 tools and save time via rapid access to information with AI tools \[34,50\]. Furthermore, concretizing the SDGs addressed in the study with AI-supported tools facilitated the teaching of complex topics. Pre-service teachers expressed that they made abstract concepts more understandable thanks to the “visual/creative content” support offered by AI.

Content Knowledge (CK): One of the most striking findings of the study emerged in the Content Knowledge (CK) dimension. In quantitative analyses, no statistically signifi- cant difference was found between the pre-test and post-test scores in the CK dimension (_p_ \> 0.05). Furthermore, the calculated small effect size (_d_ = 0.33) objectively confirms that the intervention had a limited practical impact on deepening the candidates’ subject matter expertise compared to the technical dimensions. However, in qualitative inter- views, pre-service teachers stated that they accessed information faster and could simplify topics using AI tools. This suggests that AI functioned primarily as an ‘information re- triever and reorganizer’, improving access and processing skills rather than as a ‘deep knowledge constructor’.

The disparity between the modest increase in CK and the substantial growth in AI-TK and AI-TPK can be attributed to the nature of the intervention. Acquiring deep domain ex- pertise in complex interdisciplinary topics like SDGs requires a longer cognitive maturation process than acquiring operational skills in using digital tools. The 10-week intervention focused heavily on the ‘instrumental’ and ‘design’ aspects of AI (how to prompt, how to cre- ate visuals), which explains the rapid growth in technological and pedagogical dimensions. This suggests that AI serves as a powerful accelerator for methodological competence (how

to teach) but cannot instantly replace the need for extensive study to build substantive knowledge (what to teach).

More specifically, teacher candidates developed digital materials on scattered and various SDG topics (e.g., one group focused on Climate Action while another on Gender Equality) throughout the process. Their selection of diverse SDG topics indicates that their cognitive focus was directed more towards mastering the AI-supported technologies rather than deepening their expertise in a single SDG domain. Consequently, while AI tools successfully scaffolded the material production process, they did not automatically generate new domain expertise in the absence of intensive, content-focused instruction. If future studies are conducted by selecting specific, narrowing SDG-focused topics, it is likely that competence in SDG content would also improve alongside technological skills.

Pedagogical Knowledge (PK) and AI-TPK: A significant increase was observed in the pre-service teachers’ PK and AI-TPK scores. Qualitative data indicated that AI tools offered “student-centered teaching”, “instant feedback”, and “differentiated instruction” opportunities. Materials prepared with tools, especially those like Alayna and Kahoot, facilitated offering content suitable for students’ individual learning speeds and styles. This finding parallels the determination of Jiang et al. \[54\] that AI technologies can provide instant feedback to students. Furthermore, An et al. \[55\] state that integrating AI technical knowledge with pedagogical knowledge supports students’ self-directed learning. In the study, pre-service teachers’ utilization of AI in differentiated instruction and assessment processes proves that their pedagogical competencies are blended with technology. Addi- tionally, Louly \[22\] emphasizes that AI tools transform pedagogy by providing personalized learning experiences and automated assessment. In this study, pre-service teachers used AI not just as a presentation tool but as a pedagogical assistant (e.g., generating questions, creating scenarios) while teaching SDG goals.

AI-Technological Knowledge (AI-TK): In the quantitative findings, a significant in- crease favoring the post-test was seen in the AI-TK dimension. In qualitative data, this situ- ation was supported by themes of “discovering new tools”, “technological self-confidence”, and “digital literacy”. Pre-service teachers increased their technological competencies by using generative AI tools (DeepSeek, Alayna, ChatGPT) and AI-supported Web 2.0 tools (Canva, Kahoot) that they had not used or had used very little before. This finding parallels the result of Hava and Babayigit˘ \[44\] that digital proficiency is a significant predictor of AI-TPACK competencies and that familiarity with technology increases teachers’ tendency to use AI tools. Moreover, pre-service teachers’ direct interaction with AI tools to produce materials during the implementation process increased their levels of using technological tools as “content creators” and positively affected their attitudes towards technology, as stated by Ku¸s-Gürbey and Büyük \[[7\]](#references).

Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) and AI-Technological Content Knowledge (AI-TCK): Significant differences were also detected in the PCK and AI-TCK dimensions. Pre-service teachers gained competence in the pedagogy of reducing SDG topics to a level students can understand and blending this with technology. In qualitative data, pre-service teachers stated that their pedagogy and technology competencies developed with the emphasis on “concretizing concepts” and “visualization”. For example, their visualization and concretization of an abstract subject like “Life Below Water” (SDG 14) via Canva or Prezi is compatible with Koçulu’s \[45\] emphasis on the importance of effective teaching strategies and material development in SDG teaching. Ning et al. \[42\] state that AI-TCK enables teachers to provide immersive and interactive learning experiences to students using AI; the infographic and gamification applications in this study confirm this finding.

AI-Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK): The most important result of the study is the significant increase in the overall AI-TPACK score, which is sup-

ported by a ‘large’ effect size (_d_ = 0.93). This high magnitude indicates that the training did not merely result in a statistical difference but led to a substantial practical transformation in how pre-service teachers blend technology, pedagogy, and content. This situation shows that pre-service teachers have started to view technology, pedagogy, and SDG content not as independent parts but as complementary elements. UNESCO \[[13\]](#references) emphasizes the use of AI compatible with human-centered and sustainable development goals in the AI competency framework for teachers. This study proved that pre-service teachers could develop their digital competencies while creating SDG awareness using AI tools. Sensitivity to SDG issues increases when Web 2.0 tools and AI applications are used together \[56\]. As stated by Xu et al. \[57\], teachers’ positive attitudes and self-efficacy towards AI play a critical role in their AI-TPACK development. Expressions such as “fun learning”, “increased motivation”, “digital literacy”, and “technological self-confidence” in the qualitative data show that this training process positively affected pre-service teachers’ attitudes towards AI and strength- ened their intentions to use these technologies in their future classrooms. Tram \[43\] states that AI-TPACK is a strong factor affecting AI self-efficacy and performance expectancy. Additionally, Bae et al. \[58\] determined that training given to pre-service teachers reduces anxiety towards AI technologies while increasing awareness.

While the findings highlight significant gains in AI-TPACK, a critical reading is nec- essary regarding the risks of ‘pedagogical automation’. The ease and efficiency reported by participants (e.g., rapid lesson planning with Alayna) carry the risk of technological dependence, where teachers might prioritize AI-generated suggestions over their own peda- gogical reasoning. The role of the teacher must remain that of a critical mediator rather than a passive operator of digital tools. Furthermore, given the single-group quasi-experimental design of this study, the observed positive outcomes should be interpreted with analytical caution. The ‘novelty effect’ of using cutting-edge AI tools (ChatGPT, DeepSeek) for the first time may have inflated participants’ motivation and self-efficacy scores. It is possible that the enthusiasm stems partly from the technological fascination rather than solely from deep pedagogical integration. Future longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these competencies persist once the novelty of the technology fades.

The research was conducted as a single-group experimental study and possesses inherent limitations regarding internal validity, such as potential maturation or historical effects. However, the triangulation provided by the explanatory sequential mixed-methods design mitigates these concerns. Qualitative findings explicitly attribute the observed gains to specific intervention activities such as the use of the ‘Alayna’ AI tool for lesson planning rather than natural maturation processes. Given the complexity of the AI tools introduced, it is unlikely that the substantial increases observed in AI-TK (d = 0.69) and AI-TPACK (d = 0.93) occurred solely due to the passage of time. A second significant limitation concerns the study group, which comprised 31 s-year pre-service teachers from a single university. This demographic homogeneity restricts the generalizability of the findings to broader teacher education contexts. Nevertheless, consistent with the research design, the primary objective was ‘depth of inquiry’ rather than broad generalization. The relatively small sample size facilitated a granular analysis of digital artifacts (e.g., lesson plans, infographics) and detailed qualitative coding of peer feedback processes, which would have been methodologically unmanageable with a larger cohort. Consequently, these findings should be interpreted as context-specific evidence derived from an intensive pilot intervention, serving as a baseline for future multi-centered studies.

6. **Conclusions**

Consequently, the integration of AI-supported Web 2.0 tools into teacher education has increased pre-service teachers’ awareness of global problems such as SDGs while signif-

icantly improving their capacity to teach these subjects by blending them with technology (AI-TPACK). It can be said that the applied training in this study enabled pre-service teachers to view technology not as a “barrier” but as a “tool” supporting their profes- sional development.

The study was carried out within the scope of the Instructional Technologies course, which is a compulsory course at the second-year level of the faculty of education. The biggest limitation of the study is the absence of another class to be evaluated as a control group at the same level. To minimize this limitation, pre-service teachers conducted peer assessments in the classroom environment. Possible errors in the material development process were detected instantly, and the quality of the instructional intervention was standardized by focusing on the process, not just the final product. Therefore, although there was no experimental control group, an attempt was made to methodologically ensure the internal validity of the study and the reliability of the findings by performing multiple evaluations.

While the results indicate significant improvements in AI-TPACK scores, these find- ings rely on ‘perceived competence’ self-reports rather than direct observations of classroom performance. Given the single-group quasi-experimental design, it is not possible to assert a strong causal link solely attributed to the AI tools. The observed increases may par- tially result from the ‘novelty effect’, where participants’ enthusiasm is driven by their first-time exposure to cutting-edge tools like ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Furthermore, the guided context of the university course provides a safe environment that differs from the complexities of real K-12 classrooms. Therefore, the transferability of these competencies to actual teaching practice should be interpreted with caution. The study demonstrates immediate formative gains, but long-term retention and application require further longi- tudinal investigation.

_Recommendations_ The results of this research showed that AI and AI-supported Web 2.0 tools are effective

in developing pre-service teachers’ AI-TPACK competencies, but different approaches are needed in some areas, such as Content Knowledge (CK). In this context, the following recommendations are presented for practitioners, policymakers, and researchers.

Increasing Design-Oriented and Applied Training: Study findings showed that the active role of pre-service teachers in the digital material development process significantly increased their Technological Knowledge (AI-TK) and Technological Pedagogical Knowl- edge (AI-TPK). For this reason, instead of theoretical knowledge transfer in teacher training programs, design-based courses where pre-service teachers produce concrete products using AI tools (ChatGPT, Canva, Alayna, etc.) can be expanded.

Focusing on the Integration of Technology with Content Knowledge (CK): No quanti- tatively significant difference was found in the CK dimension in the study. As stated by Ning et al. \[42\], the development of non-technical knowledge elements (CK) may require more complex processes compared to technical elements. Therefore, specific modules can be added on how to use AI tools not only as a presentation or material preparation tool but also to deepen subject matter knowledge (for example, explaining complex physics concepts with simulation or analyzing interdisciplinary topics such as SDGs).

Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) Integration: The study showed that AI facili- tates the teaching of complex and abstract topics (e.g., Climate Action, Life Below Water) such as SDGs. Koçulu \[45\] states that teachers experience difficulties while planning SDG topics. In this context, interdisciplinary outcomes where AI and Sustainability Education are blended can be defined in curriculum programs to use AI-supported tools as a lever in the teaching of interdisciplinary topics.

Updating Digital Competence Standards: Hava and Babayigit˘ \[44\] determined that digital proficiency is a significant predictor of AI-TPACK. Teacher competency frameworks can be updated to cover “Artificial Intelligence Literacy” and “AI-Supported Pedagogical Competence”, not just basic computer literacy.

Longitudinal Studies: This study covers a 10-week process. Longer-term follow-up studies should be conducted to see the persistence of the AI-TPACK skills gained by pre- service teachers and how they are reflected in the classroom environment when they start the profession.

Mixed Methods and Qualitative Deepening: To better understand the reasons for the quantitative non-significance in the CK dimension, analyses examining the cognitive processes pre-service teachers experience while creating content with AI can be performed. Furthermore, as stated by Xu et al. \[57\], studies with broader participation examining the mediating role of teachers’ attitudes towards AI can be conducted.

Comparisons in Different Disciplines: This study was conducted on a specific group. Future research can examine whether the pedagogical integration styles of AI tools differ for pre-service teachers in Verbal (Social Studies, Turkish) and Numerical (Science, Math) fields.
